nodes.name: Index set [M]
nodes.statement: $[M]$ defines the set $\{1,\dots,M\}$, with $|\cdot|$ indicating the size or cardinality of a set.

nodes.name: Sub-vector notation x_A
nodes.statement: For a set $A = \{a,b,c\}$, denote ${\mathbf{x}}_A \coloneq ({\mathbf{x}}_a,{\mathbf{x}}_b,{\mathbf{x}}_c)$, and thus ${\mathbf{x}}_{[N]} \coloneq ({\mathbf{x}}_1,{\mathbf{x}}_2,\dots,{\mathbf{x}}_N)$.

nodes.name: Leave-one-out vector notation
nodes.statement: The notation ${\mathbf{x}}^{\backslash{i}}_{[N]} \coloneq ({\mathbf{x}}_1,\dots,{\mathbf{x}}_{i-1},{\mathbf{x}}_{i+1},\dots,{\mathbf{x}}_N)$ represents the vector that omits the $i$-th element, with a similar format applied to the matrix ${\mathbf{X}}_A$ and ${\mathbf{X}}^{\backslash{i}}_{A}$.

nodes.name: Variance of a function
nodes.statement: The variance $\mathrm{var}(f) = \mathbb{E} [f({\mathbf{x}})^2] - (\mathbb{E} [f({\mathbf{x}})])^2$ for a function $f$ over a random variable ${\mathbf{x}}$.

nodes.name: Fractional independent vertex cover and fractional chromatic number
nodes.statement: Given a graph $G = (V,E)$, where $V$ and $E$ represent the set of vertices and edges of the graph $G$, respectively. Then, there exists a set $\mathcal{D}_{G} = \{ (I_j, \omega_j) \}_{j \in [J]}$, where $I_j \subseteq V$ and $\omega_j \in (0,1]$, which is a fractional independent vertex cover of $G$, if satisfying the following: \begin{enumerate}[(1)] \setlength\itemsep{-0.2pt} \vspace{-0.1in} \item each vertex is painted thoroughly, ensuring there are no overlaps or omissions, i.e., $\forall v \in V, \ \sum_{j: v \in I_j} \omega_j = 1$; \item every \( I_j \) is an independent set of vertices, which means that no two vertices in \( I_j \) are connected. \end{enumerate} \vspace{-0.1in} Define the fractional chromatic number $\chi_{f}(G) = \min_{\mathcal{D}_{G}} \sum_j \omega_j$, which is the minimum value among all fractional independent vertex covers of $G$.
differentia: each vertex is painted thoroughly, ensuring there are no overlaps or omissions, i.e., $\forall v \in V, \ \sum_{j: v \in I_j} \omega_j = 1$
every \( I_j \) is an independent set of vertices, which means that no two vertices in \( I_j \) are connected.
nodes.statement_short: A weighted family of independent sets covering each vertex with total weight 1; $\chi_f(G)$ is the minimum total weight.
nodes.label: def:fractional vertex cover appendix

nodes.name: Dependency graph
nodes.statement: A series of random variables ${\mathbf{X}} = ({\mathbf{x}}_i)_{i=1}^N$ over $\mathcal{X}$, can be associated with a corresponding dependency graph $G = (V, E)$ that illustrates the dependencies between the variables. Then, the graph $G$ satisfies the following: \begin{enumerate}[(1)] \setlength\itemsep{-0.2pt} \vspace{-0.1in} \item $V = [N]$; \item an edge \((j, k) \in E\) exists if and only if the random variables \({\mathbf{x}}_j\) and \({\mathbf{x}}_k\) are dependent. \end{enumerate} \vspace{-0.1in}
differentia: an edge \((j, k) \in E\) exists if and only if the random variables \({\mathbf{x}}_j\) and \({\mathbf{x}}_k\) are dependent.
nodes.label: def: dependency graph

nodes.name: Fractionally colorable function
nodes.statement: Given random variables \({\mathbf{X}} = ({\mathbf{x}}_1, \ldots, {\mathbf{x}}_N) \in \mathcal{X}^N\) with its dependency graph $G = (V, E)$. A function $f: \mathcal{X}^N \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is a fractionally colorable function w.r.t. the graph $G$ if there exists a decomposition $\mathcal{D}_{G}(f) = \{ (f_{j}, I_{j}, \omega_{j}) \}_{j \in [J]}$, satisfying: \begin{enumerate}[(1)] \setlength\itemsep{-0.2pt} \vspace{-0.1in} \item the set \(\{ (I_{j}, \omega_{j}) \}_{j \in [J]}\) constitutes a fractional independent vertex cover of the graph \(G\); \item the function $f$ can be decomposed as \(f({\mathbf{X}}) = \sum_{j \in [J]} \omega_j f_j ({\mathbf{x}}_{I_j})\) , where $f_j: \mathcal{X}^{|I_j|} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, \( \forall j \in [J]\). \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: A function of graph-dependent variables that decomposes as a weighted sum of functions on the independent sets of a fractional cover.
nodes.label: def: franctionally colorable single

nodes.name: Multi-fractionally sub-additive function
nodes.statement: Given $m$ random variables ${\mathbf{X}} = ({\mathbf{X}}_1, {\mathbf{X}}_2, \dots, {\mathbf{X}}_K)$ with $K$ blocks, where for each $k \in [K]$, random variables ${\mathbf{X}}_k$ is associated with a dependency graph \(G_k = ([m_k], E_k)\), and $\sum_{k \in [K]} m_k = m$. A function $f: \mathcal{X}^{m} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is \emph{multi-fractionally sub-additive} w.r.t. $\{G_k\}_{k=1}^K$ if it can be expressed as $f({\mathbf{X}}) = \sum_{k \in [K]} f_k({\mathbf{X}}_k)$, where each $f_k: \mathcal{X}^{m_k} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is fractionally colorable w.r.t. $G_k$ with a decomposition $\mathcal{D}_{G_k}(f_k) = \{ (f_{kj}, I_{kj}, \omega_{kj}) \}_{j \in [J_k]}$, and each $f_{kj}$ is sub-additive (see the detailed definition in Appendix~\ref{sec_app:material_sub_additive}).
nodes.statement_short: A sum over K blocks of fractionally colorable functions whose pieces $f_{kj}$ are sub-additive.
nodes.label: def: franctionally colorable multi

nodes.name: Multi-Task Learning with Multi-Graph Dependent data (MTL-MGD) setup
nodes.statement: Here, we introduce the learning setup of \textbf{Multi-Task Learning with Multi-Graph Dependent data (MTL-MGD)}. Given a training dataset \( S = \{({\mathbf{x}}, y)\}_{i=1}^{m} \) that is organized into \( K \) blocks (or tasks), such that \( S = (S_1, \dots, S_K) \). Each block \( S_k = \{({\mathbf{x}}_{ki}, y_{ki})\}_{i=1}^{m_k} \) is drawn from a distribution \( D_k \) (for \( k \in [K] \)) over the domain \( \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y} \) and is associated with a dependency graph \( G_k \), with \( \sum_{k \in [K]} m_k = m \).
definiendum: Multi-Task Learning with Multi-Graph Dependent data (MTL-MGD)
nodes.statement_short: Training set split into K tasks, task k drawn from $D_k$ with its own dependency graph $G_k$.

nodes.name: Multi-task hypothesis h
nodes.statement: Let a hypothesis be ${h} \coloneq ({h}_1, \dots, {h}_K)$, where each individual mapping \( {h}_k: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \widetilde{\mathcal{Y}} \) corresponds to a particular task \( k \in [K] \).

nodes.name: Hypothesis space H
nodes.statement: Denote $\mathcal{H} \coloneq \left \{ h \right \}$ as the hypothesis space.

nodes.name: Task hypothesis space H_k and loss function L
nodes.statement: For each $k \in [K]$, $\mathcal{H}_k \coloneq \left \{{h}_k ~|~ {h}_k: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \widetilde{\mathcal{Y}} \right \}$, and define a loss function as $L: \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y} \times \mathcal{H}_k \rightarrow \mathbb{R}_+$.

nodes.name: Empirical and expected risk
nodes.statement: For each ${h} \in \mathcal{H}$, define its empirical risk $\widehat{R}_{S}(h)$ on dataset $S$ and expected risk $R(h)$, with their clear and simple symbols, as follows, respectively: \begin{align} P_m (L_h) \overset{\textup{def}}{=} \widehat{R}_{S}(h) = \frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^K \frac{1}{m_k} \sum_{i=1}^{m_k} L({\mathbf{x}}_{ki}, y_{ki}, h_k) , \quad P (L_h) \overset{\textup{def}}{=} R(h) = \mathbb{E}_{S} \left[ \widehat{R}_{S}(h) \right] . \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Empirical risk is the task-averaged mean loss; expected risk is its expectation over S.

nodes.name: Weighted empirical and expected averages P_m g and P g
nodes.statement: Similarly, for a function $g = (g_1,\dots, g_K)$, where $g_k: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}, \forall k \in [K]$, we can define $P_m (g)$ and $P (g)$, simplified as $P_m g$ and $P g$, as follows, respectively: \begin{align} P_m g \overset{\textup{def}}{=} P_m (g) = \frac{1}{K} \sum_{k \in [K]} \sum_{j \in J_k} \frac{\omega_{kj}}{m_k} \sum_{i \in I_{kj}} g_k({\mathbf{x}}_i), \quad P g \overset{\textup{def}}{=} P (g) = \mathbb{E} [P_m (g)]. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Fractional-cover-weighted empirical average $P_m g$ of a multi-task function and its expectation $P g$.

nodes.name: MTL-MGD expected risk minimization
nodes.statement: The objective of MTL-MGD is to learn a hypothesis $h$ that minimizes the expected risk $P (L_h)$.

nodes.name: Existence of an optimal hypothesis h*
nodes.statement: For the distribution $D = (D_1, \dots, D_K)$, assume that there exists an optimal hypothesis $h^*=(h_1^*,\dots,h_K^*) \in \mathcal{H}$, satisfying $P (L_{h^*}) = \inf_{h \in \mathcal{H}} P (L_h)$.

nodes.name: Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) algorithm A
nodes.statement: In addition, in this paper, we consider the practical learning algorithm based on the Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) rule, as follows: \begin{align} \mathcal{A}: \ \hat{h} = \mathrm{argmin}_{h \in \mathcal{H}} P_m(L_h) . \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: ERM: return the hypothesis minimizing the empirical risk $P_m(L_h)$ over $\mathcal{H}$.

nodes.name: Multi-task function class F
nodes.statement: First, we give the following function class considered within this subsection: \begin{align} \mathcal{F} = \{ f: (f_1,f_2,\dots,f_K)~|~f_k: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}, \forall k \in [K] \}. \end{align}

nodes.name: Assumption 1 (loss function: Lipschitz and Bernstein condition)
nodes.statement: Suppose a loss function satisfies the following conditions: \begin{enumerate}[(1)] \setlength\itemsep{-0.2pt} \item $L$ is $\mu $-Lipschitz continuous, i.e., $\forall k \in [K], i \in [m_k]$, $|L({\mathbf{x}}_{ki},y_{ki},h_k')-L({\mathbf{x}}_{ki},y_{ki},h_k'')| \leq \mu |h_k'({\mathbf{x}}_{ki})-h_k''({\mathbf{x}}_{ki})|$, where $h_k', ~h_k'' \in \mathcal{H}_k$; \item There is a constant $B > 1$ such that $\forall h \in \mathcal{H}, P(h-h^*)^2 \leq BP(L_h-L_{h^*})$.~\footnote{Note that this condition is usually met from a uniform convexity condition of $L$. In later applications of Macro-AUC and experiments, we assume $L \in [0, B]$, making this condition follow, which is easily met in practice. } \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Loss is $\mu$-Lipschitz and satisfies $P(h-h^*)^2 \le B P(L_h-L_{h^*})$.
nodes.label: thm:assump2

nodes.name: Local fractional Rademacher complexity (LFRC)
nodes.statement: Assume $\mathcal{F}$ is defined in Eq.~\eqref{eq:function_class_f}.~\footnote{Note that the function class can cover both the widely-used hypothesis space and loss space.} For a fixed $r$, the LFRC of $\mathcal{F}$ can be defined as \begin{align} \mathcal{R} (\mathcal{F},r) = \mathbb{E} _{S \sim D^m_{[K]}} [ \hat{\mathcal{R}} (\mathcal{F},r) ], \end{align} where $S \sim D^m_{[K]}$ denotes $S_1 \sim D^{m_1}_1,S_2 \sim D^{m_2}_2,...,S_K \sim D^{m_K}_K$ for simplicity, and the empirical LFRC $\hat{\mathcal{R}} (\mathcal{F},r)$ can be defined as \begin{align} \hat{\mathcal{R}} (\mathcal{F},r) = \frac{1}{K} \mathbb{E} _\zeta \left [ \sup _{f \in \mathcal{F},\mathrm{var}(f_k) \leq r, k \in [K]} \sum_{k \in [K]} \frac{1}{m_k} \sum_{j \in [J_k]} \omega_{kj} \sum_{i \in I_{kj}} \zeta_l f_k({\mathbf{x}}_i)\right ], \end{align} where $\zeta_1,\zeta_2,...,\zeta_m$ is a sequence of independent Rademacher variables: $\mathbb{P} (\zeta_l = 1) = \mathbb{P} (\zeta_l = -1) = \frac{1}{2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Expected supremum of fractional-cover-weighted Rademacher sums over functions with per-task variance at most r.
nodes.label: def: LFRC

nodes.name: Base bound of MGD with small variance (analog of Bartlett et al. Thm 2.1)
nodes.statement: Assume the function class $\mathcal{F}$ is defined in Eq.~\eqref{eq:function_class_f}. Assume that there is some $r>0$ for every $f \in \mathcal{F}$, $\mathrm{var}(f_k) \leq r$, $\max_{k \in {K}} \sup_{{\mathbf{x}}} |f_k({\mathbf{x}})| \leq 1$. Then for every $t > 0$, with probability at least $1-e^{-t}$, \begin{align*} \sup_{f \in \mathcal{F}} (P f - P_m f) \leq \inf_{\alpha > 0} \left(2(1 + \alpha) \mathcal{R} (\mathcal{F} , r) + \sqrt {\frac{2crt}{K}} + (\frac{2}{3} + \frac{1}{\alpha})\frac{ct}{K} \right) , \end{align*} where $c=\frac{5^2}{4^2} \sum_k \frac{\chi_f(G_k)}{m_k}$. Moreover, the same results hold for the quantity $\sup _{f \in \mathcal{F}} (P _m f - P f)$. For every $t> 0 $, with probability at least $1-e^{-t}$, \begin{align*} \sup _{f \in \mathcal{F}} (P _m f - P f) \leq \inf_{\alpha > 0} \left(2(1 + \alpha) \mathcal{R} (\mathcal{F} , r) + \sqrt {\frac{2crt}{K}} + (\frac{2}{3} + \frac{1}{\alpha})\frac{ct}{K} \right) . \end{align*}
assumptions: Assume the function class $\mathcal{F}$ is defined in Eq.~\eqref{eq:function_class_f}.
there is some $r>0$ for every $f \in \mathcal{F}$, $\mathrm{var}(f_k) \leq r$, $\max_{k \in {K}} \sup_{{\mathbf{x}}} |f_k({\mathbf{x}})| \leq 1$
conclusions: the same results hold for the quantity $\sup _{f \in \mathcal{F}} (P _m f - P f)$
nodes.statement_short: With prob. $1-e^{-t}$, the uniform deviation is bounded by $2(1+\alpha)$LFRC plus $\sqrt{2crt/K}$ and $ct/K$ terms, with $c$ depending on $\chi_f(G_k)/m_k$.
nodes.label: thm:the core 2.1

nodes.name: Remark on Theorem 1 tightness and i.i.d. case
nodes.statement: This theorem shows the maximum difference between the empirical and the expected value, which is associated with LFRC and the small variance of the class. This theorem is the main basis of the following theoretical results. Further, we can analyze the tightness of our results: when $K = 1$, our result has one more constant $\frac{5^2}{4^2}$, which cannot cover the i.i.d. case~\cite{Bartlett_2005}. But if we use Theorem \ref{thm:bennett_inequality_refined} (see Appendix \ref{sec-app:a_special_bennett_inequality}), our result can cover i.i.d. case.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 1 is the basis of later results; for K=1 it carries an extra constant $5^2/4^2$, removable via Theorem 5.

nodes.name: Improved bound of MGD with sub-root function
nodes.statement: Assume that there are some functional $T : \mathcal{F}_k \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^+$ and some constant $B$, for all $f \in \mathcal{F}, T(f_k) \in [\mathrm{var}(f_k), B\mathbb{E} f_k]$. If a sub-root function $\Phi$ and its fixed point $r^*$ satisfy:~\footnote{Notably, here the content in $\{\}$ of $\mathcal{R}\{\}$ means adding some conditions to the function class (e.g., $T(f_k) \leq r$).} \begin{align} \forall r \geq r^*, ~ \Phi (r) \geq B \mathcal{R} \{ f \in \mathcal{F}, T(f_k) \leq r \}. \end{align} Then for each $f\in \mathcal{F}$, $M >1$ and $t > 0$, with probability at least $1 - e^{-t}$, the following holds: \begin{align} P f \leq \frac{M}{M-1} P _m f + \frac{c_1 M}{B} r^* + (c_2 BM +22 ) \frac{ct}{K}, \end{align} where $c_1 = 704$, $c_2 = 26$, and $c = \frac{5^2}{4^2} \sum_{k \in K}\frac{\chi_f(G_k)}{m_k} $.
assumptions: there are some functional $T : \mathcal{F}_k \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^+$ and some constant $B$, for all $f \in \mathcal{F}, T(f_k) \in [\mathrm{var}(f_k), B\mathbb{E} f_k]$
a sub-root function $\Phi$ and its fixed point $r^*$ satisfy:
\forall r \geq r^*, ~ \Phi (r) \geq B \mathcal{R} \{ f \in \mathcal{F}, T(f_k) \leq r \}.
conclusions: P f \leq \frac{M}{M-1} P _m f + \frac{c_1 M}{B} r^* + (c_2 BM +22 ) \frac{ct}{K},
nodes.statement_short: Fixed-point bound: $Pf \le \frac{M}{M-1}P_m f + \frac{704M}{B} r^* + O(ct/K)$ when a sub-root $\Phi$ dominates B times the localized LFRC.
nodes.label: thm: theorem 3.3 sub-root

nodes.name: Remark on fixed-point analysis
nodes.statement: Subsequent analyses of the fixed point facilitate practical applications of inequalities.

nodes.name: Excess risk bound of A for MTL-MGD
nodes.statement: Assume the loss function satisfies Assumption \ref{thm:assump2}. There exists a sub-root function $\Phi$ and its fixed point $r^*$, satisfying \begin{align*} \forall r \geq r^*, ~ \Phi (r) \geq B \mu \mathcal{R} \{ h \in \mathcal{H}, \mu^2 \mathbb{E} (h_k - h_k^*)^2 \leq r \}. \end{align*} Then for every $t > 0$ and $ r \geq \Phi(r)$, with probability at least $1 - e^{-t}$, \begin{align} P (L_ {\hat{h}} - L_{h^*}) \leq \frac{c_1 }{B} r + (c_2 B + 22) \frac{ct}{K}, \end{align} where $c_1 = 704$, $c_2 = 26$ and $c = \frac{5^2}{4^2} \sum_{k \in K}\frac{\chi_f(G_k)}{m_k}$.
assumptions: Assume the loss function satisfies Assumption \ref{thm:assump2}.
There exists a sub-root function $\Phi$ and its fixed point $r^*$, satisfying
\forall r \geq r^*, ~ \Phi (r) \geq B \mu \mathcal{R} \{ h \in \mathcal{H}, \mu^2 \mathbb{E} (h_k - h_k^*)^2 \leq r \}.
$t > 0$ and $ r \geq \Phi(r)$
nodes.statement_short: Excess risk of the ERM hypothesis is at most $\frac{704}{B} r + (26B+22)ct/K$ for any $r \ge \Phi(r)$.
nodes.label: thm : Lipschitz bound loss space

nodes.name: Rate depends on the order of r
nodes.statement: From the corollary, we can observe that the rate of the risk bound is intrinsically linked to the order of $r$.

nodes.name: Excess risk bound of kernel-based learning algorithm A
nodes.statement: Suppose a loss function $L$ satisfies Assumption \ref{thm:assump2}. Assume $\sup _{{\mathbf{x}} \in \mathcal{X}} \kappa({\mathbf{x}},{\mathbf{x}}) < \Lambda$ and for every $k \in [K]$, $f_k = \theta_k^T \phi({\mathbf{x}}_k)$, where a weight vector satisfies $\|\theta_k\|_2 \leq \widetilde{M}$, and $\phi: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathbb{H}$. For all $t > 0$, with probability at least $1 - e^{-t}$, we have \footnote{$a$ $\lesssim$ $b$ means $a$ $\leq$ $Cb$, where $C$ is a constant.} \begin{align} P (L_{\hat{h}} - L_{h^*}) \lesssim r^* + \frac{ t}{K} \sum_{k \in [K]} \frac{\chi_f(G_k)}{m_k}, \end{align} where \begin{align} r^* \leq \sum _{k \in [K]} \min _{d_k \geq 0} \left( \frac{d_k \chi_f(G_k)}{K m_k} + \widetilde{M} \sqrt{\frac{\chi_f(G_k)}{K m_k} \sum _{l >d_k} \lambda_{kl}} \right). \end{align}
assumptions: Suppose a loss function $L$ satisfies Assumption \ref{thm:assump2}.
$\sup _{{\mathbf{x}} \in \mathcal{X}} \kappa({\mathbf{x}},{\mathbf{x}}) < \Lambda$
for every $k \in [K]$, $f_k = \theta_k^T \phi({\mathbf{x}}_k)$, where a weight vector satisfies $\|\theta_k\|_2 \leq \widetilde{M}$, and $\phi: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathbb{H}$
nodes.statement_short: For kernel classes the excess risk is $\lesssim r^* + \frac{t}{K}\sum_k \chi_f(G_k)/m_k$, with $r^*$ bounded via kernel eigenvalue tails.
nodes.label: thm: loss bound computing

nodes.name: Order of r* in n for kernel hypotheses
nodes.statement: From this corollary, we discuss the order of $r^*$ w.r.t. $n$ (and $K$). For simplicity, assume $m_1 = \dots = m_K = n$, and denote $d_k^* = \mathrm{argmin}_{d_k \geq 0} \frac{d_k \chi_f(G_k)}{K m_k} + \widetilde{M} \sqrt{\frac{\chi_f(G_k)}{K m_k} \sum _{l >d_k} \lambda_{kl}}$. \begin{enumerate}[(1)] \setlength\itemsep{-0.4pt} \item When for each $k \in [K], d_k^* = 0$, $r^* \leq \sum_k \widetilde{M} \sqrt{\frac{\chi_f(G_k)}{K n} \mathrm{trace}(\kappa_k)}$, we can obtain $r^* = O(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}})$ (or $O\left(\sqrt{\frac{1}{n K} (\sum_k \chi_f(G_k))(\sum_k \mathrm{trace}(\kappa_k))}\right)$). Specifically, in this case, $r^* \lesssim \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}} \cdot \sqrt{(\sum_k \frac{\chi_f(G_k)}{K}) (\sum_k \mathrm{trace} (\kappa_k))} $ (see details in Proposition~\ref{pro: kernel proof1}). \item When for some $k$, $d_k^* \neq 0$, and the rank of kernel matrix $\mathrm{Rank}(\kappa_k) < \infty$, we can obtain $r^* = O(\frac{1}{n})$ (or $O\left( \frac{1}{n K} \sum_k \mathrm{Rank}(\kappa_k) \chi_f(G_k) \right)$). Specifically, we can choose $d_k' < \infty$ and $\sum_{l >d_k'} \lambda_{kl} = 0$ (i.e., $d_k' \geq \mathrm{Rank}(\kappa_k)$), thus $r^* \leq \sum_k \frac{\mathrm{Rank}(\kappa_k) \chi_f(G_k)}{K n}$. There are many kernels of finite rank, such as linear kernel, and we can take $d_k' = a$, where $a$ is a constant. \item When for every $k \in [K]$, ${\{\lambda_{kl}\}}_{l = 1}^{\infty} $ has the property of exponential decay, i.e., $\sum_{l >d_k'} \lambda_{kl} = O(e^{-d_k'})$ (e.g., the Gaussian Kernel), by setting the truncation threshold at $d_k' = \log n$, we can obtain $r^* = O(\frac{\log n}{n})$ or $O\left( \max\{\sum_k \frac{\log n \chi_f(G_k)}{n K} , \sum_k \sqrt{\frac{\chi_f(G_k)}{n^2 K}}\}\right)$. Specifically, in this case, $r^* \lesssim \sum_k \frac{\log n \chi_f(G_k)}{K n} + \sum_k \sqrt{\frac{\chi_f(G_k)}{n K} e^{-\log n} } \lesssim \sum_k \frac{\log n \chi_f(G_k)}{n K}+ \sum_k \sqrt{\frac{\chi_f(G_k)}{n^2 K}}$. If $K \leq \log n \chi_f(G_k)$, then $r^* =O\left( \sum_k \frac{\log n \chi_f(G_k)}{n K} \right) $, else $r^* = O\left( \sum_k \sqrt{\frac{\chi_f(G_k)}{n^2 K}} \right)$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Rates of $r^*$: $O(1/\sqrt n)$ in general, $O(1/n)$ for finite-rank kernels, $O(\log n/n)$ for exponentially decaying spectra.

nodes.name: Multi-graph dependent random variables setup
nodes.statement: \textbf{Setup.} Consider $m$ random variables ${\mathbf{X}} = ({\mathbf{X}}_1, {\mathbf{X}}_2, \dots, {\mathbf{X}}_K)$ with $K$ blocks, where for each $k \in [K]$, random variables ${\mathbf{X}}_k$ is associated with a dependency graph \(G_k = ([m_k], E_k)\), and $\sum_{k \in [K]} m_k = m$.

nodes.name: Multi-fractionally sub-additive function f in setup

nodes.name: Assumption 2 (properties of the function of MGDV)
nodes.statement: Suppose $f$ is multi-fractionally sub-additive w.r.t. $\{G_k\}_{k=1}^K$, then for every $f_k$ has a decomposition $\mathcal{D}_{G_k}(f_k) = \{ (f_{kj}, I_{kj}, \omega_{kj}) \}_{j \in [J_k]}$. Besides, assume every $k \in [K], ~ j \in [J_k]$ satisfy the following conditions: \begin{enumerate}[(1)] \setlength\itemsep{-0.4pt} \item for every ${\mathbf{x}}_{I_{kji}}$, where $i \in I_{kj}$, there exists a $\sigma({\mathbf{x}}_{I_{kj}})$- measurable random variable $Y_{kji}$ associated with it. Moreover, $Y_{kji}$ satisfies: $\mathbb{P} (Y_{kji} \leq Z_{kj} - Z_{kj}^{\backslash{i}} \leq 1) = 1$, and $\mathbb{P} \left( \mathbb{E}_{kji}[Y_{kji}] \geq 0 \right) = 1,$ where \(\mathbb{E}_{kji}\) represents the expectation relative to the \(\sigma\)-algebra formed by \(({\mathbf{x}}_{I_{kj}^{\backslash{\{i\}}}})\); \item for every ${\mathbf{x}}_{I_{kj}}$, there exists constraint values $b_{kj},~\sigma_{kj}^2 \in \mathbb{R}$, satisfying $\mathbb{P} (Y_{kji} \leq b_{kj}) = 1$, and $\mathbb{P} \left( \sigma_{kj}^2 \geq \sum_{i \in I_{kj}} \mathbb{E}_{kji}[Y_{kji}^2] \right) = 1;$ \item let $v_{kj} \overset{\textup{def}}{=} (1 + b_{kj}) \mathbb{E}[Z_{kj}] + \sigma_{kj}^2$, and $v_{kj} \in \mathbb{R}$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Bennett-type inequality for multi-graph dependent variables
nodes.statement: Assume $Z$ is defined as Eq.\eqref{def :Z def}, and can be described as $Z = \sum_{k \in [K]} \sum_{j \in [J_k]} \omega_{kj} Z_{kj}$. Suppose Assumption~\ref{thm:assump1} holds, and for each $k \in [K]$, $j \in [J_k]$, $b_{kj} = b$. Then, \begin{enumerate}[(1)] \item for every $t > 0$, \begin{align} \mathbb{P} (Z \geq \mathbb{E}[Z] + t) \leq \exp \left( -\frac{v}{W} \varphi \left( \frac{tW}{Uv}\right) \right) \leq \exp \left( - \frac{v}{ \sum_{k \in [K]} \chi_{f} (G_k)} \varphi \left( \frac{4t}{5v}\right) \right) , \end{align} where $\varphi$ is defined in Eq.\eqref{eq:psi_function}, $v = (1 + b) \mathbb{E} [Z] + \sigma^2$, $\sigma^2 = \sum_k \sum_j \omega_{kj} \sigma_{kj}^2$, $W = \sum_{k \in [K]} \chi_f(G_k) = \sum_{k \in [K]} \omega_k$, and $U = \sum_{k \in [K]} U_k$, $U_k = \sum_{j \in J_k} \max (1, v_{kj}^{\frac{1}{2}} W^{\frac{1}{2}} v^{-\frac{1}{2}})$; \item for every $t > 0$,~\footnote{Note that, Eq.~\eqref{eq:thm_bennet_2} is usually called the Bernstein-type inequality~\cite{concentration13initial}.} \begin{align} \mathbb{P} (Z \geq \mathbb{E}[Z] + \sqrt{2cvt} + \frac{2ct}{3}) \leq e^{-t} , \end{align} where $c = \frac{5^2}{4^2} \sum_{k \in [K]} \chi_{f} (G_k)$. \end{enumerate}

assumptions: Assume $Z$ is defined as Eq.\eqref{def :Z def}, and can be described as $Z = \sum_{k \in [K]} \sum_{j \in [J_k]} \omega_{kj} Z_{kj}$.

nodes.name: Theorem 3 generalizes single-graph Bennett inequality
nodes.statement: This is a more general Bennett inequality, encompassing the single-graph dependent one in~\cite{ralaivola2015entropy} when $K = 1$. Especially, if $\omega_{kj} = 1$ for $k \in [K], ~j \in [J_k]$, then a special Bennett's inequality can be obtained (see detailed in Theorem \ref{thm:bennett_inequality_refined} of Appendix \ref{sec-app:a_special_bennett_inequality}). Technically, Eq.~\eqref{eq:thm_bennet_2} is due to the employing of various common shrinking techniques, i.e., $\varphi(x) \geq \frac{x^2}{2+\frac{2x}{3}}$.~\footnote{Note that, using the existing literature \cite{yousefi18,watkins2023optimistic}, we can only derive a constant of $\frac{2}{3}$ instead of $\frac{1}{3}$ (owing to the original literature \cite{bousquet2002bennett} does not provide detailed steps to prove this), but this does not affect the order of bounds.}

nodes.name: Talagrand-type inequality for empirical process
nodes.statement: Let a function class $\mathcal{F} = \{ f = (f_1, f_2, \ldots, f_K) \}$, where each $f_k: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, and assume that all functions $f_k$ are measurable, square-integrable, and fulfill the conditions $\mathbb{E} [f_k({\mathbf{x}}_{kj})] = 0$ for all $k \in [K]$ and $j \in [m_k]$. Besides, we require that $\|f_k\|_{\infty} \leq 1$, i.e., $\sup_{{\mathbf{x}}} |f_k({\mathbf{x}})| \leq 1$. Define $Z$ as follows: \begin{align*} Z \overset{\textup{def}}{=} \sup_{f \in \mathcal{F}} \sum_{k \in [K]} \sum_{j \in [J_k]} \omega_{kj} \sum_{i \in I_{kj}} f_k({\mathbf{x}}_i). \end{align*} Furthermore, for each $k \in [K]$ and $j \in [J_k]$, let $\sigma_{kj}$ represent a positive real value such that $\sigma_{kj}^2 \geq \sum_{i \in I_{kj}} \sup_{f \in \mathcal{F}} \mathbb{E} [f^2({\mathbf{x}}_i)]$. Then, for every $t \geq 0$, \begin{align} \mathbb{P} (Z \geq \mathbb{E}[Z] + t) \leq \exp \left( - \frac{v}{ \sum_{k \in [K]} \chi_{f} (G_k)} \varphi \left( \frac{4t}{5v}\right) \right) , \end{align} where $v = \sum_{k \in [K]} \sum_{j \in [J_k]} \omega_{kj} \sigma_{kj}^2 + 2 \mathbb{E} [Z]$. Also, with probability at least $1 - e^{-t}$, \begin{align} Z \leq \mathbb{E}[Z] + \sqrt{2cvt} + \frac{2ct}{3} , \end{align} where $c = \frac{5^2}{4^2} \sum_{k \in [K]} \chi_{f} (G_k)$.

nodes.name: Original multi-label dataset
nodes.statement: This requires constructing a multi-task dataset \(S\) from the original multi-label dataset \(\widetilde{S} = \{ (\widetilde{{\mathbf{x}}}_i, \widetilde{{\mathbf{y}}}_i) \}_{i=1}^{\tilde{n}}\), where \( \widetilde{{\mathbf{x}}}_i \in \widetilde{\mathcal{X}}\), \(\widetilde{{\mathbf{y}}}_i \in \{ -1, +1 \}^K\), and \( \widetilde{y}_{ki} = 1 \) ( or \(-1\)) indicates the label \( k\) is relevant (or irrelevant).

nodes.name: Positive/negative instance sets and imbalance level factor tau_k
nodes.statement: Besides, for each \(k \in [K]\), let \(\widetilde{S}_k^+ = \{ \widetilde{{\mathbf{x}}}_p | \widetilde{y}_{pk} = 1, \forall p \in [\tilde{n}]\}\) and \(\widetilde{S}_k^- = \{ \widetilde{{\mathbf{x}}}_p | \widetilde{y}_{pk} = -1, \forall p \in [\tilde{n}]\}\) denote the sets of positive and negative instances, respectively, and denote \(\tilde{n}_k^+ = | \widetilde{S}_k^+ |, \tilde{n}_k^- = | \widetilde{S}_k^- | \), and \(\tau_k = \frac{\min \{ \tilde{n}_k^+, \tilde{n}_k^- \}}{n}\) is the imbalance level factor for simplicity.

nodes.name: Macro-AUC optimization
nodes.statement: The goal is to learn the best original multi-label hypothesis \( \tilde{h} \in \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) from \(\widetilde{S}\) to maximize the Macro-AUC metric \( \mathbb{E}_{\widetilde{S}} \left[ \frac{1}{K} \sum_{k \in [K]} \frac{1}{\tilde{n}_k^+ \tilde{n}_k^-} \sum_{ (\widetilde{{\mathbf{x}}}_p, \widetilde{{\mathbf{x}}}_q) \in \widetilde{S}_k^+ \times \widetilde{S}_k^-} \tilde{L} (\widetilde{{\mathbf{x}}}_p, \widetilde{{\mathbf{x}}}_q, \tilde{h}_k ) \right] \), where \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} = \{(\tilde{h}_1,\tilde{h}_2,\dots, \tilde{h}_K) | \tilde{h}_k: \widetilde{\mathcal{X}} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}, \forall k \in [K]\} \) and $\tilde{L}$ denotes a loss function.

nodes.name: Macro-AUC to MTL-MGD transformation
nodes.statement: In the transformation, each label is treated as an individual task, leading to \(S = \{ S_k \}_{k=1}^K\), with \(S_k = \{ ({\mathbf{x}}_{kj}, y_{kj}) \}_{j=1}^{m_k}\). Specifically, for each label (or task) $k \in [K]$, each instance \({\mathbf{x}}_{kj}\) (\(j \in [m_k]\)) is formed from a positive and negative sample (i.e., \( {\mathbf{x}}_{kj} = (\widetilde{{\mathbf{x}}}_p, \widetilde{{\mathbf{x}}}_q), \forall (\widetilde{{\mathbf{x}}}_p, \widetilde{{\mathbf{x}}}_q) \in \widetilde{S}_k^+ \times \widetilde{S}_k^- \)), and its label \(y_{kj} = 1\), and thus the total number of instances is \(m_k = \tilde{n}_k^+ \tilde{n}_k^- = \tilde{n}^2 \tau_k (1 - \tau_k)\). Besides, the transformed hypothesis \( h_k({\mathbf{x}}_{kj}) = \tilde{h}_k(\widetilde{{\mathbf{x}}}_p) - \tilde{h}_k(\widetilde{{\mathbf{x}}}_q)\).
nodes.statement_short: Each label becomes a task whose instances are positive-negative pairs, $m_k = \tilde n^2\tau_k(1-\tau_k)$, $h_k$ a score difference.

nodes.name: Fractional chromatic number of the bipartite ranking dependency graph
nodes.statement: Then, we can get the dependency graph \(G_k\) of \(S_k\) based on prior results in bipartite ranking \cite{ralaivola2015entropy} satisfying: $\forall k \in [K], \chi _f(G_k) = \max \{|\tilde{n}_k^+|,|\tilde{n}_k^-|\} = (1- \tau _k) \tilde{n}.$
nodes.statement_short: The pair dependency graph of task k has $\chi_f(G_k) = \max(n_k^+, n_k^-) = (1-\tau_k)\tilde n$.

nodes.name: Sub-additive function
nodes.statement: Given a function $f: \mathcal{X}^N \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, it is sub-additive when the following holds: there exists $N$ functions, i.e., $ f_1,\dots, f_N$, where $f_i : \mathcal{X}^{N-1} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}, \forall i \in [N]$, such that $\sum_{i=1}^N \left( f ({\mathbf{X}}) - f_i ({\mathbf{X}}^{\backslash{i}}) \right) \leq f ({\mathbf{X}})$, where the definition of ${\mathbf{X}}^{\backslash{i}}$ can be seen in Section \ref{section: preliminaries}, i.e., ${\mathbf{X}}^{\backslash{i}} = ({\mathbf{x}}_1, \dots, {\mathbf{x}}_{i-1}, {\mathbf{x}}_{i+1}, \dots, {\mathbf{x}}_N)$.

nodes.name: Sub-root function
nodes.statement: A function \( \Phi : [0, \infty) \rightarrow [0, \infty) \) is said to be sub-root if it is nonnegative, nondecreasing, and for every \( r > 0 \), the mapping function \( r \mapsto \frac{\Phi(r)}{\sqrt{r}} \) is nonincreasing. We will only focus on nontrivial sub-root functions, meaning those that are not the constant function \( \Phi \equiv 0 \).

nodes.name: Property of sub-root functions (fixed point)
nodes.statement: If a function \( \Psi : [0, \infty) \rightarrow [0, \infty) \) is a nontrivial sub-root function, then it is continuous throughout the interval \( [0, \infty) \), and the equation \( \Phi(r) = r \) has a solitary positive solution $r^*$, which is called fixed point. Furthermore, for every positive value of \( r \), it follows that \( r \geq \Phi(r) \) $\Longleftrightarrow$ \( r^* \leq r \).

nodes.name: Theorem 5 complements Theorem 3
nodes.statement: This theorem serves as a complement to Theorem \ref{thm:bennett_inequality} and represents a specific instance of the Bennett inequality, applicable to i.i.d random variables. A detailed analysis and discussion of its implications will follow.

nodes.name: Comparison of refined Bennett inequality with i.i.d. and single-graph cases
nodes.statement: Discussion: then we discuss the above inequality in two cases, and in contrast to the i.i.d. case \cite{Bartlett_2005,yousefi18,watkins2023optimistic} and the single graph \cite{ralaivola2015entropy}. \begin{enumerate}[(1)] \item in the i.i.d. case, $\chi _f(G_k) = \chi _f(G) = 1 $, we take $K = 1$ to contrast to single-graph, \\ the result in the single-graph case is \begin{align*} \mathbb{P} (Z - \mathbb{E} Z \geq t) \leq e^{-\frac{v}{\chi _f(G)} \varphi (\frac{4t}{5v})} = e^{-v \varphi (\frac{4t}{5v})}, \end{align*} while our result is \begin{align*} \mathbb{P} (Z - \mathbb{E} Z \geq t) \leq e^{-v \varphi (\frac{t}{v \sum _{k \in [K]} \chi _f(G_k)})} = e^{-v \varphi (\frac{t}{v})}. \end{align*} For a fixed $t$, we observe that the smaller $ \mathbb{P} (Z - \mathbb{E} Z \geq t) $ this term, the better. Since $\varphi (\frac{t}{v}) > \varphi (\frac{4t}{5v})$, $e^{-v \varphi (\frac{t}{v})} < e^{-v \varphi (\frac{4t}{5v})}$, our bound is tighter, and Bennett's inequality in prior work can be viewed as a special case. \item in the graph-dependent case, $\chi_f(G) \neq 1$, we also take $K =1$ to contrast to the single-graph. In this case, $\sum _{k \in [K]} \chi _f(G_k) = \chi _f(G) \geq 2$, \\ the result in \cite{ralaivola2015entropy} is \begin{align*} \mathbb{P} (Z - \mathbb{E} Z \geq t) \leq e^{-\frac{v}{\chi _f(G)} \varphi (\frac{4t}{5v})}, \end{align*} while our result is \begin{align*} \mathbb{P} (Z - \mathbb{E} Z \geq t) \leq e^{-v \varphi (\frac{t}{v \sum _{k \in [K]} \chi _f(G_k)})} = e^{-v \varphi (\frac{t}{v \chi _f(G)})}. \end{align*} Denote $\clubsuit _1 = -\frac{v}{\chi _f(G)} \varphi (\frac{4t}{5v}) $, and $ \clubsuit _2 = -v \varphi (\frac{t}{v \chi _f(G)}) $, $c_1 = \frac{1}{\chi _f(G)}$, $c_2 = \frac{4}{5}$, $x = \frac{t}{v}$, then \begin{align*} \clubsuit_1 - \clubsuit _2 = & v \varphi (c_1 x) - c_1 v \varphi (c_2 x) = v (\varphi (c_1 x) - c_1 \varphi(c_2 x) ) \\ = & (1 +c_1 x)\log (1+c_1 x) - c_1(1 +c_2x) \log (1+ c_2 x) - (c_1 - c_1 c_2)x. \end{align*} We can notice that as $\chi _f(G)$ increases, $\clubsuit _1 - \clubsuit_2 $ becomes smaller and smaller, i.e., $\clubsuit _1 - \clubsuit _2 \approx 0 $. Thus our result in Theorem \ref{thm:bennett_inequality_refined} is equivalent to the result in \cite{ralaivola2015entropy}. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: For K=1 the refined inequality is tighter than the single-graph one in the i.i.d. case and asymptotically equivalent as $\chi_f(G)$ grows.

Also, with probability at least $1 - e^{-t}$, \begin{align} Z \leq \mathbb{E}[Z] + c \sqrt{2vt} + \frac{2ct}{3} , \end{align} where $c = \sum_{k \in [K]} \chi_{f} (G_k)$.

nodes.statement: Given $Z = \sum_{k \in [K]} \sum_{j \in [J_k]} \omega_{kj}Z_{kj} $ (see details in Eq.\eqref{def :Z def}, Section \ref{section: main results}). Suppose Assumption \ref{thm:assump1} holds, and for every $k \in [K], j \in [J_k]$, $b_{kj}=b, ~\omega_{kj}=1$. Then for all $t>0$, \begin{align} \mathbb{P} (Z \leq \mathbb{E}[Z] - t) \leq \exp \left( - \frac{v}{W} \varphi \left( \frac{tW}{Uv} \right) \right) \leq \exp \left( -\frac{v}{\sum_{k \in [K]} \chi_f(G_k) } \varphi \left(\frac{4t}{5v} \right) \right) , \end{align} where $\varphi$ is defined as above, i.e., $\varphi(x)=(1+x) \log(1+x)-x$. Owing to the fact $x \geq 0$, $\varphi(x) \geq \frac{x^2}{2+ \frac{2x}{3}}$, we can get \begin{align} \mathbb{P} (Z \leq \mathbb{E} [Z] - \sqrt{2cvt} - \frac{2ct}{3}) \leq e^{-t}, \end{align} where $c = \frac{5^2}{4^2} \sum_{k \in [K]} \chi_f(G_k)$. The definition of $v,~W,~U$ can be seen in Theorem \ref{thm:bennett_inequality}.

nodes.name: Two-sided Bennett inequality and its tightness
nodes.statement: This theorem supplements the Bennett inequality and can be used to analyze the lower bounds of the generalization bounds discussed later. Furthermore, this theorem can be combined with the results of Theorem \ref{thm:bennett_inequality}, then $\mathbb{P} (|Z - \mathbb{E} [Z]| \geq t) \leq 2 \exp ( -\frac{v}{\sum_{k \in [K]} \chi_f(G_k)} \varphi (\frac{4t}{5v} ) )$. The equivalence of the upper and lower bounds implies that the bound obtained is relatively tight. However, the result does not cover the i.i.d. case. This indicates that the result is not optimal and that there is still a gap $\frac{5}{4}$ to be bridged.
nodes.statement_short: Combining upper and lower tails gives $P(|Z-EZ|\ge t) \le 2\exp(\cdot)$; a factor 5/4 gap to the i.i.d. case remains.

Thus \begin{align*} \mathbb{P} (Z \geq \mathbb{E}[Z] & + t) \leq \exp \left( -\frac{v}{W} \varphi \left( \frac{tW}{Uv}\right) \right) \notag \\ \leq \exp & \left( - \frac{v}{ \sum_{k \in [K]} \chi_{f} (G_k)} \varphi \left( \frac{4t}{5v}\right) \right). \end{align*} Since $x \geq 0, \varphi (x) \geq \frac{x^2}{2+\frac{2x}{3} } $, inequality (\eqref{eq:thm_bennet_2}) is deduced.

nodes.statement: Because of $\omega_{kj}=1$, we can get $\omega_k = |J_k| \in [1,m_k]$, every ${\mathbf{x}}_{kj}$ in only one independent set. Then we can define $p_k,q_{kj}$ and some constants as the following: \begin{align*} & \sigma^2 = \sum_{k \in [K]} \sum_{j \in [J_k]} \omega_{kj} \sigma_{kj}^2, \ v = (1 + b) \mathbb{E} [Z] + \sigma^2, p_k = \frac{U_k}{U}, U = \sum _{k \in [K]} U_k, \\ & c = \sum_{k \in [K]} \chi_{f} (G_k), \ \chi_{f} (G_k) \overset{\textup{def}}{=} \sum_{j \in [J_k]} \omega_{kj}, q_{kj} = \frac{1}{U_k}, U_k = \sum _{j \in [J_k]} = \omega_k . \end{align*} Review the proof of the Theorem \ref{thm:bennett_inequality}, we can get: \begin{align} \mathbb{P} (Z - \mathbb{E} Z \geq t) \leq e^{(\log \sum _{k \in [K]} p_k \sum _{j \in [J_k]} q_{kj} (v_{kj} \psi (-\frac{\lambda}{p_k q_{kj}})) - \lambda t)}, \end{align} then \begin{align*} v_{kj} \psi (-\frac{\lambda}{p_k q_{kj}}) = v_{kj} \psi (- \lambda U) \overset{\text{\ding{172}}}{\leq} v \psi (- \lambda U), \end{align*} the inequality \text{\ding{172}} is due to every $v_{kj} \geq 0$, $v = \sum _{k \in [K]} \sum _{j \in [J_k]} v_{kj} \geq v_{kj} $. Finally, we can get the one part in Theorem \ref{thm:bennett_inequality_refined}, and the second part in Theorem \ref{thm:bennett_inequality_refined} is due to the fact $x \geq 0$, $\varphi (x) \geq \frac{x^2}{2 + \frac{2x}{3}}$.

Then \begin{align*} V^+ & \leq \mathbb{E} V^+ + \sqrt{\frac{2c(r + 2\mathbb{E} V^+) t}{K}} +\frac{2ct}{3K} \\ & \overset{\text{\ding{172}}}{\leq} \mathbb{E} V^+ +\sqrt {\frac{4c \mathbb{E} V^+ t}{K}} + \sqrt {\frac{2crt}{K}} + \frac{2ct}{3K} \\ & \overset{\text{\ding{173}}}{\leq} (1+\alpha) \mathbb{E} V^+ + \sqrt {\frac{2crt}{K}} + (\frac{2}{3} + \frac{1}{\alpha})\frac{ct}{K} \\ & \overset{\text{\ding{174}}}{\leq} 2(1 + \alpha) \mathcal{R} (\mathcal{F} , r) + \sqrt {\frac{2crt}{K}} + (\frac{2}{3} + \frac{1}{\alpha})\frac{ct}{K}, \\ \end{align*} where \text{\ding{172}} is due to the fact $\sqrt{a + b} \leq \sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b}$, i.e., $\sqrt{\frac{2c(r + 2\mathbb{E} V^+) t}{K}} \leq \sqrt {\frac{4c \mathbb{E} V^+ t}{K}} + \sqrt {\frac{2crt}{K}} $, and \text{\ding{173}} is due to the fact $\forall \alpha > 0, 2 \sqrt{ab} \leq \frac{a}{\alpha} + \alpha b$, and we can combine similar items. \text{\ding{174}} is due to the proposition \ref{pro: equ Rademacher}.

We can notice $\frac{r}{w(f_k)} \in [0,1]$, then for each $g \in \mathcal{G}_r, \| g_k\|_ \infty \leq 1$, and we found $\mathrm{var}(g_k) \leq r$. Because \begin{itemize} \item $T(f_k) \leq r$, then \begin{align*} a = 0, w(f) = 1, \forall g \in \mathcal{G}_r, g = f , \mathrm{var}(g_k) = \mathrm{var}(f_k) \leq r; \end{align*} \item $T(f_k) >r$, then \begin{align*} g = \frac{f}{\lambda^a}, T(f_k) \in (r \lambda^{a-1}, r\lambda^a], \mathrm{var}(g_k) = \frac{\mathrm{var}(f_k)}{\lambda^{2a}} \leq r. \end{align*} \end{itemize} Then we can apply Theorem \ref{thm:the core 2.1} for $\mathcal{G}_r$, for all $x > 0$, with probability $1 - e^{-t}$, \begin{align*} V_r^+ \leq 2(1+\alpha) \mathcal{R}(\mathcal{G}_r) +\sqrt{\frac{2crt}{K}} + (\frac{2}{3} +\frac{1}{\alpha}) \frac{ct}{K}. \end{align*} Then \begin{align*} \mathcal{R}(\mathcal{G}_r) = \frac{1}{K} \left[ \mathbb{E}_ {\mathbf{x}} \mathbb{E} _\zeta \underbrace{ \sup _{g \in \mathcal{G}_r,\mathrm{var}(g_k) \leq r} \sum_{k \in [K]} \frac{1}{m_k} \sum_{j \in J_k} \omega_{kj} \sum _{i \in I_{kj}} \zeta_l g_k(x_i) }_\spadesuit \right]. \end{align*} Let $T(f_k) \leq Bb$, define $a_0$ to be the smallest integer that $r\lambda^{a_0+1} \geq Bb $ and partition $\mathcal{F}(0,Bb) $, i.e., $\mathcal{F}(0,r) + \mathcal{F}(r\lambda^0,r \lambda^1) +\mathcal{F}(r\lambda^1,r \lambda^2),...(r\lambda^{a_0}, r \lambda^{a_0+1}) $, then \begin{align*} \spadesuit & \leq \sup_{g \in \mathcal{G}_r, T(f_k) \in [0,r]} \sum_{k \in [K]} \frac{1}{m_k} \sum_{j \in J_k} \omega_{kj} \sum _{i \in I_{kj}} \zeta_i g_k(x_i) +\sup _{g \in \mathcal{G}_r, T(f) \in [r,Bb]} \sum_{k \in [K]} \frac{1}{m_k} \sum_{j \in J_k} \omega_{kj} \sum _{i \in I_{kj}} \zeta_i g_k(x_i) \\ & = \sup _{f \in \mathcal{F}(0,r)} \sum_{k \in [K]} \frac{1}{m_k} \sum_{j \in J_k} \omega_{kj} \sum _{i \in I_{kj}} \zeta_i f_k(x_i) + \sup _{f \in \mathcal{F}(r,Bb)} \sum_{k \in [K]} \frac{1}{m_k} \sum_{j \in J_k} \omega_{kj} \sum _{i \in I_{kj}} \zeta_i \frac{r}{w(f_k)} f_k(x_i) \\ & \leq \sup _{f \in \mathcal{F}(0,r)} \sum_{k \in [K]} \frac{1}{m_k} \sum_{j \in J_k} \omega_{kj} \sum _{i \in I_{kj}} \zeta_i f_k(x_i) + \sum _{j=0} ^{a_0} \sup _{f \in \mathcal{F}(r\lambda ^j, r \lambda ^{j+1})} \sum_{k \in [K]} \frac{1}{m_k} \sum_{j \in J_k} \omega_{kj} \sum _{i \in I_{kj}} \zeta_i \frac{r}{r\lambda^j} f_k(x_i) \\ & = \sup _{f \in \mathcal{F}(0,r)} \sum_{k \in [K]} \frac{1}{m_k} \sum_{j \in J_k} \omega_{kj} \sum _{i \in I_{kj}} \zeta_i f_k(x_i) + \sum _{j=0} ^{a_0} \frac{1}{\lambda^j} \sup _{f \in \mathcal{F}(r\lambda ^j, r \lambda ^{j+1})} \sum_{k \in [K]} \frac{1}{m_k} \sum_{j \in J_k} \omega_{kj} \sum _{i \in I_{kj}} \zeta_i f_k(x_i). \end{align*} Since the property in Definition~\ref{lemma: sub-root def}, i.e., $\forall \gamma \geq 1, \Phi(\gamma r) \leq \sqrt{\gamma} \Phi(r)$, then we can get: \begin{align*} \mathcal{R}(\mathcal{G}_r) & \leq \mathcal{R} \mathcal{F} (0,r) + \sum _{j=0} ^{a_0} \frac{1}{\lambda^j} \mathcal{R} \mathcal{F}(r \lambda^j, r \lambda^{j+1} ) \leq \frac{\Phi(r)}{B} + \frac{1}{B} \sum _{j=1} ^{a_0} \frac{1}{\lambda^j} \Phi (r \lambda^{j+1}) \\ & \leq \frac{\Phi(r)}{B} + \frac{1}{B} \sum _{j=1} ^{a_0} \frac{1}{\lambda^j} \lambda^{\frac{j+1}{2}} \Phi (r) = \frac{\Phi(r)}{B} \left[ 1 + \sqrt{\lambda} \sum _{j=0}^{a_0} \frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda^j}} \right], \end{align*} then taking $\lambda = 4$, we can get: \begin{align*} \mathcal{R}(\mathcal{G}_r) \leq \frac{5\Phi(r)}{B}. \end{align*} Since the property in Definition~\ref{lemma: sub-root def} and Lemma \ref{lemma:sub-root pro}, i.e., $\Phi(r^*) = r^*$, and $\frac{\Phi(r)}{\sqrt{r}}$ is nonincreasing, thus \begin{align*} V_r^+ & \leq 2(1+\alpha) \frac{5\Phi(r)}{B} +\sqrt{\frac{2crt}{K}} + (\frac{2}{3} +\frac{1}{\alpha}) \frac{ct}{K} \\ & \leq \frac{10(1+\alpha)}{B} \sqrt{r r^*} + \sqrt{\frac{2crt}{K}} + (\frac{2}{3} +\frac{1}{\alpha}) \frac{ct}{K}. \end{align*} Then let $A = \frac{10(1+\alpha)}{B} \sqrt{r^*} + \sqrt{\frac{2ct}{K}} $, $C = (\frac{2}{3} +\frac{1}{\alpha}) \frac{ct}{K} $, thus \begin{align*} V_r^+ \leq A \sqrt{r} + C. \end{align*} Then we can apply lemma 3.8 \sqrt{ab} \leq \frac{1}{2}(\beta a + \frac{b}{\beta})$, then \begin{align*} P f & \leq \frac{M}{M-1} P _m f + \lambda BMA^2 +2C \\ & = \frac{M}{M-1} P _m f + \lambda B M (\frac{100(1+\alpha)^2 r^*}{B^2} + \frac{20(1+\alpha)}{B} \sqrt{\frac{2cr^*t}{K}} + \frac{2ct}{K}) + (\frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{\alpha}) \frac{2ct}{K}, \\ & \leq \frac{M}{M-1} P _m f + \lambda B M \left[\frac{100(1+\alpha)^2 r^*}{B^2} + \frac{20(1+\alpha)}{B} \left(\frac{1}{2} ( \frac{5r^*}{B} + \frac{2cBt}{5K}) \right) + \frac{2ct}{K} \right] + (\frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{\alpha}) \frac{2ct}{K}, \\ \end{align*} let $\alpha = \frac{ct}{K}, \\ \end{align*} where $c = \frac{5^2}{4^2} \sum _{k \in [K]} \frac{\chi_f(G_k)}{m_k}$. Let $c_1 = 704$, $c_2 = 26$, then we can get inequality \eqref{eq: thm sub-root 3.3_1}. <\frac{\chi_f(G_k)}{K m_k} \zeta_k \phi ({\mathbf{x}}_k) , \varphi _{kl} > \varphi _{kl}> \\ + & <\theta_k, \sum _{l > d_k} <\frac{\chi_f(G_k)}{K m_k} \zeta_k \phi ({\mathbf{x}}_k), \varphi _{kl} >, nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 2
nodes.statement: We can notice that \begin{align*} \mathcal{R}\{ h \in \mathcal{H}, \mu^2 \mathbb{E} (h_k - h_k^*)^2 \leq r \} & = \mathcal{R}\{ h \in \mathcal{H}, \mathbb{E} (h_k - h_k^*)^2 \leq \frac{r}{\mu ^2} \} = \mathcal{R}\{ h-h^*, h \in \mathcal{H}, \mathbb{E} (h_k - h_k^*)^2 \leq \frac{r}{\mu ^2} \} \\ & \leq \mathcal{R}\{ h - g, h,g \in \mathcal{H}, \mathbb{E} (h_k - g_k^*)^2 \leq \frac{r}{\mu ^2} \} = 2 \mathcal{R}\{ h, h \in \mathcal{H}, \mathbb{E} h_k ^2 \leq \frac{r}{4 \mu ^2} \}, \end{align*} We define a function $\Psi(r) = \frac{\widetilde{c}_1}{2} \mathcal{R}\{ h \in \mathcal{H}, \mu^2\mathbb{E} (h_k - h_k^*)^2 \leq r \}+\frac{11\mu^2 t}{m}$, $\widetilde{c}_1 = 2B\mu$. $\Psi(r)$ is a sub-root function (owing to Lemma~3.4 in \cite{Bartlett_2005}). Then use the Proposition~\ref{thm:kernel upper bound}, we can get \begin{align*} \Psi(r) \leq \sum_{k \in [K]} \left( \frac{2 \chi_f(G_k)}{K m_k} \sum_{l=1}^{\infty} \min\{\frac{r}{4 \mu^2},\widetilde{M}^2 \lambda_{kl}\} \right)^{\frac{1}{2}} + \frac{11 \mu^2 t}{m}. \end{align*} Similar to \cite{Bartlett_2005} (i.e., adding a constant $c$ to a sub-root function can increase its fixed point by at most $2c$), it suffices to show that \begin{align*} r \leq 2B\mu \sum_{k \in [K]} \left( \frac{2 \chi_f(G_k)}{K m_k} \sum_{l=1}^{\infty} \min\{\frac{r}{4\mu^2},\widetilde{M}^2 \lambda_{kl}\} \right)^{\frac{1}{2}}. \end{align*} Then \begin{align*} r \leq C \left[ \sum_{k \in [K]} \min _{0 \leq d_k \leq m_k} \left( \frac{1}{2 \mu} \sqrt{\frac{r d_k \chi_f(G_k)}{K m_k}} +\widetilde{M} \sqrt{\frac{\chi_f(G_k)}{K m_k} \sum _{l > d_k} \lambda _{kl}} \right) \right]. \end{align*} Since $r \geq \Psi(r)$ and the property in Lemma \ref{lemma:sub-root pro}, i.e., the fixed point $r^*$ satisfied $r^* = \Psi(r^*)$. Then \begin{align*} r ^* \leq C \left[ \sum_{k \in [K]} \min _{0 \leq d_k \leq m_k} \left( \frac{1}{2 \mu} \sqrt{\frac{r d_k \chi_f(G_k)}{K m_k}} +\widetilde{M} \sqrt{\frac{\chi_f(G_k)}{K m_k} \sum _{l > d_k} \lambda _{kl}} \right) \right], \end{align*} where $C$ is a constant about $B, \mu$.

nodes.name: Convergence analysis of the linear Macro-AUC bound
nodes.statement: With inequality \eqref{eq:linear eq AUC}, we can notice that $P(L_{\hat{h}} - L_{h^*}) = O(r^*) + O(\frac{1}{K \tilde{n}}) $, similarly, $r^* \in [O(\frac{1}{\tilde{n}}), O(\sqrt{\frac{1}{\tilde{n}}})]$ in inequality \eqref{eq:linear r AUC}. Then we analyze $r^*$, i.e., $\frac{1}{\bar{M}^2} \cdot \frac{d'}{\tilde{n}} \sum_{k \in [K]} \frac{1}{\tau_k} + \widetilde{M} \sqrt{\frac{1}{\tilde{n}} \sum_{k \in [K]} \frac{1}{\tau_k} \sum_{l > d'} \widetilde{\lambda}_l^2 } $, by the value of $d'$, where $d' = \mathrm{argmin}_{d \geq 0} (\frac{1}{\bar{M}^2} \cdot \frac{d}{\tilde{n}} \sum_{k \in [K]} \frac{1}{\tau_k} + \widetilde{M} \sqrt{\frac{1}{\tilde{n}} \sum_{k \in [K]} \frac{1}{\tau_k} \sum_{l > d} \widetilde{\lambda}_l^2 }) $. \begin{enumerate}[(1)] \item $d' = 0$, in this case, then \begin{align*} r^* \leq \widetilde{M} \sqrt{\frac{1}{\tilde{n}} \sum_{k \in [K]} \frac{1}{\tau_k} \sum_{l > 0} \widetilde{\lambda}_l^2 } \overset{\text{\ding{172}}}{\leq} \widetilde{M} M (\sqrt{\frac{1}{\tilde{n}} \sum_{l>0} \widetilde{\lambda}_l^2 }), \end{align*} where $M = \sqrt{\sum_{k \in [K]} \frac{1}{\tau_k} }$, thus we can get the inequality \text{\ding{172}}. And we can notice that $r^* = O(\sqrt{\frac{1}{\tilde{n}}})$, which is the worst case scenario for the convergence of our generalization bounds. But we know that the generalization bound of GRC analysis is also $\sqrt{\frac{1}{\tilde{n}}}$. This at least shows that our convergence rate is not worse than GRC. \item $r(\Theta)$ is finite, where $r(\Theta)$ refers to the rank of matrix $\Theta$. then there exists $ d' < \infty $ for $\sum_{l > 0} \widetilde{\lambda}_l^2 = 0 $, then \begin{align*} r^* \leq \frac{1}{\bar{M}^2} \cdot \frac{d'}{\tilde{n}} \sum_{k \in [K]} \frac{1}{\tau_k} \overset{\text{\ding{172}}}{\leq} \frac{M^2}{\bar{M}^2} \cdot \frac{d'}{\tilde{n}}, \end{align*} where $d' = \mathrm{argmin}_{d>0} \frac{1}{\bar{M}^2} \cdot \frac{d}{\tilde{n}} $, \text{\ding{172}} is due to $M = \sqrt{\sum_{k \in [K]} \frac{1}{\tau_k} }$ (we donate). We can notice that $r^* = O(\frac{d'}{\tilde{n}})$. If $r(\Theta) \leq $, i.e., $d' \leq a$, then $r^* = O(\frac{a}{\tilde{n}})$, where $a$ is a constant. \item The eigenvalues of the SVD decomposition of the $\Theta$ matrix decay exponentially. In this case, we have $\sum_{l > d'} \widetilde{\lambda}_l^2 = O(e^{-d'})$. By setting the truncation threshold at $d' = \log \tilde{n}$, then \begin{align*} r^* \leq & (\sum_{k \in [K]} \frac{1}{\tau_k}) \cdot \frac{1}{\bar{M}^2} \cdot \frac{\log \tilde{n}}{\tilde{n}} + \widetilde{M} \sqrt{\frac{1}{\tilde{n}} \sum_{k \in [K]} \frac{1}{\tau_k} \sum_{l>d'} \widetilde{\lambda}_l^2 } \\ \leq & \frac{M^2}{\bar{M}^2} \cdot \frac{\log \tilde{n}}{\tilde{n}} + \widetilde{M} M \sqrt{\sum_{l > d'} \frac{C}{\tilde{n}^2} } \\ = & \frac{M^2}{\bar{M}^2} \cdot \frac{\log \tilde{n}}{\tilde{n}} + \widetilde{M} M \frac{\sqrt{C}}{\tilde{n}}, \end{align*} where $C$ is a constant. \text{\ding{172}} is due to the known condition and some simple deflating method used earlier. Through the above analysis, we can see that $r^* = O(\frac{\log \tilde{n}}{\tilde{n}})$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.statement: Then we can describe the setting: given dataset $S = \{S^C, S^T\}$, where $S^g = \{ S^g_1,S^g_2,...,S^g_K \}$.

nodes.name: Task subsets S_k^g
nodes.statement: For each $k \in [K]$, $S^g_k = \{ ({\mathbf{x}}_{ki}, y_{ki}, g) \}_{i=1}^{m^g_k}$.

nodes.name: Treatment/control sample sizes
nodes.statement: Also for every $k \in [K]$, $m_k = m^C_k + m^T_k$, $\sum_{k \in [K]} m_k = \sum_{k \in [K]} m_k^C + \sum_{k \in [K]} m_k^T = n^C +n^T = N$.

nodes.name: AUUC-max in multi-task learning
nodes.statement: For \( k \in [K] \), define \( h_k(S_k^T, \frac{p}{100}m_k^T) \) and \( h_k(S_k^C, \frac{p}{100}m_k^C) \) as the first \( p \) percentiles of \( S_k^T \) and \( S_k^C \), respectively, when arranged according to the predictions of each \( h_k \). Furthermore, for \( S^T \) and \( S^C \), we have \( h(S^g, \frac{p}{100} n^g) = \sum_{k \in K} h_k(S_k^g, \frac{p}{100} m_k^g) \). Then empirical AUUC of $h$ on $S$ can be defined as \begin{align*} \widehat{AUUC} (h,S) = \frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^K \int_{0}^{1} V(h_k,{\mathbf{x}}) d {\mathbf{x}} \approx \frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^K \sum_{p = 1}^{100} V(h_k,\frac{p}{100}), \end{align*} where $V(h_k,\frac{p}{100})$ satisfies the following: \begin{align*} V(h_k,\frac{p}{100}) = \frac{1}{m_k^T} \sum_{i^T \in h_k(S_k^T, \frac{p}{100}m_k^T) } y_{k i^T} - \frac{1}{m_k^C} \sum_{i^C \in h_k(S_k^C, \frac{p}{100}m_k^C) } y_{k i^C}. \end{align*} Moreover, the expected AUUC of $h$ is $\mathbb{E}_S [\widehat{AUUC}(h,S)]$.
nodes.statement_short: Empirical AUUC averages over tasks the area under the uplift curve built from treatment/control percentile responses.
nodes.label: def:multi own2 auuc

nodes.name: Relationship between AUUC-max and bipartite ranking loss in multi-task learning
nodes.statement: \textnormal{\textbf{(The relationship between AUUC-max and the bipartite ranking loss in multitask learning.)}} The definition of $\widehat{AUUC}(h,S) $ and $AUUC$ in Definition \ref{def:multi own2 auuc}. Then $AUUC$ and ranking loss satisfied the following : \begin{align*} AUUC (h) \geq \Gamma^{T,C} - \left( \Lambda^T \mathbb{E}_{S^T} [ \hat{R}(h,S^T) ] + \Lambda^C \mathbb{E}_{S^C} [ \hat{R}(h,\widetilde{S}^C) ] \right), \end{align*} where $\Gamma = \mathbb{E}_{S} [\frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^K (\bar{y}_k^T - \frac{1}{2} ((\bar{y}_k^T)^2 + (\bar{y}_k^C)^2) )]$, $\Lambda^g = \sum_{k=1}^K \bar{y}_k^g (1-\bar{y}_k^g) $, $\bar{y}_k^g = \mathbb{E} [Y_k | G=g]$.
assumptions: The definition of $\widehat{AUUC}(h,S) $ and $AUUC$ in Definition \ref{def:multi own2 auuc}.
nodes.statement_short: AUUC is lower-bounded by a constant minus weighted bipartite ranking risks on treatment and label-flipped control data.
nodes.label: pro:multi own2 ranking auuc

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 6
nodes.statement: From Definition \ref{def:multi own2 auuc}, we know the empirical AUUC of $h$, then \begin{align*} \widehat{AUUC} (h,S) = & \frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^K \int_{0}^{1} V(h_k,{\mathbf{x}}) d {\mathbf{x}} \overset{\text{\ding{172}}}{=} \frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^K \int_{0}^{1} ( F_{h_k}^{S^T_k}({\mathbf{x}}) - F_{h_k}^{S^C_k}({\mathbf{x}}) ) d {\mathbf{x}} \\ = & \frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^K \left( \int_{0}^{1} F_{h_k}^{S^T_k}({\mathbf{x}}) d {\mathbf{x}} + \int_{0}^{1} F_{h_k}^{S^C_k}({\mathbf{x}}) d {\mathbf{x}} \right) \\ \overset{\text{\ding{173}}}{=} & \frac{1}{K} \sum_{k \in [K]} ( \bar{y}_k^T (1-\bar{y}_k^T) \cdot AUC(h_k, S_k^T) + \frac{(\bar{y}_k^T)^2}{2} \\ & - \bar{y}_k^C (1-\bar{y}_k^C) \cdot AUC(h_k, S_k^C) - \frac{(\bar{y}_k^C)^2}{2} ) \\ \overset{\text{\ding{174}}}{=} & \frac{1}{K} \sum_{k \in [K]} ( \bar{y}_k^T (1-\bar{y}_k^T) \cdot AUC(h_k, S_k^T) + \frac{(\bar{y}_k^T)^2}{2} \\ & - \bar{y}_k^C (1-\bar{y}_k^C) \cdot (1 - AUC(h_k, \widetilde{S}_k^C)) - \frac{(\bar{y}_k^C)^2}{2} ) \\ \overset{\text{\ding{175}}}{=} & \frac{1}{K} \sum_{k \in [K]} ( \bar{y}_k^T (1-\bar{y}_k^T) \cdot (1 - \hat{R}_k (h_k, S_k^T)) + \frac{(\bar{y}_k^T)^2}{2} \\ & - \bar{y}_k^C (1-\bar{y}_k^C) \cdot (1 - (1 - \hat{R}_k (h_k, \widetilde{S}_k^C)) - \frac{(\bar{y}_k^C)^2}{2} ) \\ = & \frac{1}{K} \sum_{k = 1}^K ( \underbrace{ \bar{y}_k^T - \frac{1}{2} ((\bar{y}_k^T)^2 + (\bar{y}_k^C)^2) }_{\hat{\gamma}_k^{T,C}} ) - \frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^K ( \underbrace{ \bar{y}_k^T (1-\bar{y}_k^T) }_{\lambda_k^T} \hat{R}_k(h_k,S_k^T) \\ & + \underbrace{ \bar{y}_k^C (1-\bar{y}_k^C) }_{\lambda_k^C} \hat{R}_k(h_k,\widetilde{S}_k^C) ) \\ \overset{\text{\ding{176}}}{\geq} & \hat{\Gamma}^{T,C} - \left( \Lambda^T \hat{R}(h,S^T) + \Lambda^C \hat{R}(h,\widetilde{S}^C) \right). \end{align*} \text{\ding{172}} is due to \cite{aminiKDD2021uplift_Modeling,KDD2011_Ffunction}, i.e., $F_{h_k}^{S^T_k}({\mathbf{x}}), F_{h_k}^{S^C_k}({\mathbf{x}})$ can be induced by $h$, and $V(h_k,{\mathbf{x}}) = F_{h_k}^{S^T_k}(x) - F_{h_k}^{S^C_k}({\mathbf{x}})$. \text{\ding{173}} is due to \cite{aminiKDD2021uplift_Modeling,KDD2011_ginifunction}, i.e., a relationship between $F_{h_k}^D$, $Gini(h, D)$ and $AUC$, where D represents a dataset. Then we can get $\int_{0}^{1} F_{h_k}^D({\mathbf{x}}) d {\mathbf{x}} = \bar{y}_D (1-\bar{y}_D) \cdot AUC (h,D) + \frac{(\bar{y}_D)^2}{2} $, and then substitute it to \text{\ding{172}}. In \text{\ding{174}}, we revert labels in $S^C_k$ for $\forall k \in [K]$, i.e., $\widetilde{S}_k^C = \{{\mathbf{x}}_{ki},1-y_{ki},C \}_{i=1}^{m_k^C}$. Thus $AUC(h_k,S_k^C) = 1 - AUC (h_k, \widetilde{S_k^C})$ and substitute it to \text{\ding{173}}. Moreover, \text{\ding{175}} is due to the relationship between $AUC$ and empirical ranking risk, i.e., $AUC(h_k,D) = 1-\hat{R}_k(h_k,D)$, where $\hat{R}_k (h_k,D) = \frac{1}{|D^+||D^-|} \sum_{({\mathbf{x}}_{ki},{\mathbf{x}}_{kj}) \in D^+ \times D^-} [\! [h_k({\mathbf{x}}_{ki}) \leq h_k({\mathbf{x}}_{kj})]\!] $. The last inequality \text{\ding{176}} is due to $\sum_{i \in [n]} a_i b_i \leq \sum{i \in [n]} a_i \cdot \sum{i \in [n]} b_i$. Finally, we take expectations from both sides, then \begin{align*} AUUC (h) \geq \Gamma^{T,C} - \left( \Lambda^T \mathbb{E}_{S^T} [ \hat{R}(h,S^T) ] + \Lambda^C \mathbb{E}_{S^C} [ \hat{R}(h,\widetilde{S}^C) ] \right). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Write AUUC via cumulative gain curves, use the Gini-AUC relation and label flipping on control data, then take expectations.

nodes.name: Empirical risk for AUUC
nodes.statement: Then we can define our empirical risk of $h$ as follows: \begin{align*} \hat{R}_S = & \hat{R}_{S^T} + \hat{R}_{S^C}, \\ \hat{R}_{S^g} = & \frac{1}{K} \sum_{k =1}^K \frac{1}{m_k^g} \sum_{i=1}^{m_k^g} L({\mathbf{x}}_{ki},y_{ki},g,h_k), g \in \{ T,C \}. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Empirical LFRC of S^g
nodes.statement: And according to the definition of LFRC in Definition \ref{def: LFRC}, we can define the empirical LFRC of $S^g$ for $g \in \{ T,C \}$ as \begin{align*} \hat{\mathcal{R}}_{S^g}(\mathcal{H},r) = \frac{1}{K} \mathbb{E}_{\zeta} \left[ \sup_{h \in \mathcal{H},\mathrm{var}(h) \leq r} \sum_{k \in [K]} \frac{1}{m_k^g} \sum_{j \in J_k^g} \omega_{kj} \sum_{i \in I_{kj}^g} \zeta_{ki} h_k({\mathbf{x}}_{ki}) \right]. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Base theorem of AUUC-max in multi-task learning
nodes.statement: For each $t > 0$, with probability at least $1-2e^{-t}$, \begin{align*} AUUC (h) \geq & \Gamma^{T,C} - ( \Lambda^T \hat{R}(L \circ h, S^T) + \Lambda^C \hat{R}(L \circ h, S^C) ) \\ & - R_{S^T,S^C} (H,S^T,S^C) - [(\frac{2}{3} + \frac{1}{\alpha^T} ) c^T + (\frac{2}{3} + \frac{1}{\alpha^C} )c^C] \frac{t}{K} , \end{align*} where $R_{S^T,S^C} (H,S^T,S^C)$ is related to the LFRC of $S^T$ and $S^C$, i.e., $R_{S^T,S^C} (H,S^T,S^C)$ = $2(1+\alpha^T) \mathcal{R}_{S^T}(\mathcal{H},r) + \sqrt{\frac{2c^T rt}{K}} + 2(1+\alpha^C) \mathcal{R}_{S^C}(\mathcal{H},r) + \sqrt{\frac{2c^C rt}{K}}$. Additionally, $c^g = \frac{5^2}{4^2} \sum_{k \in [K]} \frac{\chi_{h,g}(G)}{m_k^g} $ for $g \in \{ T,C \}$.
conclusions: AUUC (h) \geq & \Gamma^{T,C} - ( \Lambda^T \hat{R}(L \circ h, S^T) + \Lambda^C \hat{R}(L \circ h, S^C) ) \\ & - R_{S^T,S^C} (H,S^T,S^C) - [(\frac{2}{3} + \frac{1}{\alpha^T} ) c^T + (\frac{2}{3} + \frac{1}{\alpha^C} )c^C] \frac{t}{K} ,
nodes.statement_short: With prob. $1-2e^{-t}$, AUUC is lower-bounded by empirical ranking risks minus LFRC and confidence terms.
nodes.label: thm:multi own2 2.1 base

nodes.name: Comparison of our and prior Macro-AUC excess risk bounds
nodes.statement: $h^*$ represents the minimum value of the expected risk, using techniques similar to \cite{mohri2018foundations}, then for arbitrarily $ \epsilon >0$, there exists $ h_{\epsilon}$, such that $P(L_{h_\epsilon}) \leq P(L_{h^*}) + \epsilon$. Then \begin{align*} P(L_{\hat{h}} - L_{h^*}) & = P(L_{\hat{h}}) - P(L_{h_\epsilon}) + P(L_{h_\epsilon}) - P(L_{h^*}) \leq P(L_{\hat{h}}) - P(L_{h_\epsilon}) + \epsilon \\ & = P(L_{\hat{h}}) - P_m(L_{\hat{h}}) + P_m(L_{\hat{h}}) - P(L_{h_\epsilon}) +\epsilon \\ & \overset{\text{\ding{172}}}{\leq} P(L_{\hat{h}}) - P_m(L_{\hat{h}}) + P_m(L_{h_\epsilon}) - P(L_{h_\epsilon}) +\epsilon \leq 2 \sup_{h \in \mathcal{H}} |P(L_h) - P_m (L_h)| +\epsilon , \end{align*} where $P(L_{\hat{h}} - L_{h^*})$ can be seen in Corollary \ref{thm : Lipschitz bound loss space}. \text{\ding{172}} is due to $P_m(L_{\hat{h}}) \leq P_m(L_{h_\epsilon})$. The two bounds we want to compare are as follows: \begin{align} P(L_{\hat{h}} - L_{h^*}) \leq 704 \mu r^* + \frac{75}{K} \sum_{k \in [K]} \frac{1}{\tau_k} \cdot \frac{t}{\tilde{n}}, \end{align} where \begin{align} r^* \leq 2 \min_{d \geq 0, d \in \mathbb{N}} ( \frac{1}{\bar{M}^2} \cdot \frac{d}{\tilde{n} K} \sum_{k \in [K]} \frac{1}{\tau_k} + \widetilde{M} \sum_{k \in [K]}\sqrt{\frac{1}{\tilde{n} K} \frac{1}{\tau_k} \sum_{l > d} \widetilde{\lambda}_l^2 } ), \end{align} \begin{align} P(L_{\hat{h}} - L_{h^*}) \leq 2 \left[ \frac{4 \mu \bar{M} \widetilde{M}}{\sqrt{\tilde{n}}} \left(\frac{1}{K} \sum_{k \in [K]}\sqrt{\frac{1}{\tau_k}}\right) + 3 \sqrt{\frac{\log 2 +t}{2 \tilde{n}}} \left(\sqrt{\frac{1}{K} \sum_{k \in [K]}\frac{1}{\tau_k}}\right) \right], \end{align} thus we should calculate and compare the right-hand sides of Eq. \eqref{eq: experiment our} and Eq. \eqref{eq:experiment old}. If the result of the former is smaller than that of the latter, we can approximately conclude that our bound is tighter.
